analysis.one_liner: Requires nursing homes to disclose their owners, report staffing and spending, and raises fines for harming residents.
analysis.headline: The bill received no committee vote, no floor vote, and no cosponsors before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Nursing homes today receive billions of dollars in Medicare and Medicaid payments, yet their ownership can be hidden behind layers of affiliated companies. This bill would have required facilities to disclose their owners, managers, landlords, and lenders to regulators and to anyone who asks. It would have added staffing, spending, and inspection information to the government's Nursing Home Compare website, created a standardized complaint form for residents and their families, raised fines for violations that kill or injure residents, required advance notice before a facility closes, and put independent monitors over troubled nursing home chains.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families, who would learn who actually owns and profits from a facility before trusting it with a parent's care. Taxpayers also benefit: Medicare and Medicaid cover most nursing home care in the country, so better disclosure of staffing and spending would show whether public money is going to resident care or to owners and affiliates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires skilled nursing facilities and nursing facilities to have ownership and affiliated-party information — including operators, management companies, landlords, and lenders — available on request to regulators, residents, and ombudsmen, with facilities certifying it is accurate as a condition of participating in Medicare and Medicaid [S3].

Adds prominent, searchable information to the Nursing Home Compare website, including staffing hours per resident per day, turnover, names of chronically poor 'Special Focus Facilities,' state inspection reports, and a three-year summary of enforcement actions [S3].

Raises civil money penalties to up to $100,000 for deficiencies resulting in a resident's death and $3,000–$25,000 for actual harm or immediate jeopardy, while limiting penalty reductions for repeat or serious deficiencies, and allows collected fines to fund resident relocation when a facility closes [S3].

Creates a standardized complaint form and requires states to run a complaint resolution process with tracking, investigation deadlines, and protections against retaliation against residents who complain [S3].

Requires administrators to give 60 days' written notice before a facility closes, with an approved plan to relocate every resident to an appropriate setting, and continues Medicare payments until residents are safely moved [S3].

Establishes a national independent monitor program for large nursing home chains with a record of poor care or financial problems — paid for by the chains themselves — and requires facilities part of large groups to submit annual independent audits and new owners to prove financial ability to operate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home owners and operators — particularly for-profit chains and their affiliated landlords, management companies, and lenders — who would bear the cost of disclosure, annual audits, higher fines, and independent monitoring, and could no longer keep ownership structures hidden from regulators and residents.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home owners and corporate chains

drawbacks.text: The bill's disclosure, audit, and payroll-reporting requirements impose real administrative costs on nursing facilities, and facilities could pass those costs along or close marginal facilities rather than comply, which could reduce the supply of beds in some areas [S3].

Much of the bill is reporting and study requirements rather than direct care standards — it studies aide training hours and runs demonstration projects rather than mandating more staff or higher training, so its actual effect on quality of care would depend heavily on how regulators and states implement it [S3].

The escalation of penalties up to $100,000 per deficiency falling on facilities, many of which operate on thin Medicaid margins, is a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge, even with the bill's self-reporting discount of up to 50 percent [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to a vulnerable population — elderly and disabled residents in facilities largely paid for by public insurance — in the form of transparency, stronger complaints, and real penalties for neglect. The costs are compliance burdens and fines borne by facility owners. The main design weakness is that it leans on paperwork and studies rather than hard staffing mandates, but disclosure of who owns and profits from a nursing home is a direct answer to a real problem families face: choosing care for a parent with almost no view into who is behind the facility.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2008, referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees and then to their health subcommittees, and sat there with no hearings, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Eddie Bernice Johnson of Texas introduced the bill on April 15, 2008; no other member of the House cosponsored it [S1][S4].

The House referred it to two committees, Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce, and within days it was further referred to the health subcommittee of each — a step that usually ends a bill's chances unless the subcommittee chair schedules action [S5].
No further action of any kind appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home owners and corporate chains came out ahead: they avoided the ownership disclosure, audit requirements, higher fines, and independent monitoring the bill would have imposed. Residents and families gained nothing, since the transparency provisions died before any action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.industry: For-profit nursing home operators and chains
industries.note: The bill would force them to disclose owners, landlords, and management companies, submit independent audits for large groups, prove financial viability when buying facilities, and pay fines up to $100,000 for deficiencies resulting in a resident's death. Their current interest in keeping ownership structures opaque runs directly against residents' need to know who is accountable for care [S3].

industries.industry: Nursing home landlords, management companies, and lenders
industries.note: The bill's definition of affiliated parties covers operators, landlords, management companies, lenders, and captive insurers, requiring disclosure of their role in facilities. Many of these entities profit from lease and management fees extracted from facilities, which disclosure of expenditures and ownership would expose [S3].

industries.industry: Nursing home staff, including nurses and aides
industries.note: Payroll-based staffing disclosure and dementia and abuse-prevention training would raise accountability but add paperwork; aides could benefit from the study of whether their 75-hour training minimum should increase. Their interest in adequate staffing levels aligns with resident care quality [S3].
